summary:
Caraga records no region-specific law or regulation bearing on trans people. A visitor there stands under the national framework of the Philippines, where same-sex conduct is legal nationwide and no provision of law criminalises a person for being transgender. The Caraga entry in the sourced reference material carries no separate finding on LGBT rights, so the national position governs in full.

Identity documents cannot be brought into line with a trans visitor's presentation. There is no administrative legal gender recognition: the Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. A court order is the only route, so the marker a visitor carries at hotels, checkpoints and counters will remain the one assigned at birth. A bill filed by trans Filipinos would permit applicants, including consenting minors, to choose markers other than male or female, such as X or non-binary; it had not been enacted as of the reports.

No national SOGI anti-discrimination statute is in force. The SOGIE Equality Bill has been pending in Congress since 2000 without passage, and national legislation on the subject filed since 1999 has not been enacted. Protection against discrimination exists only as a patchwork of local ordinances at barangay, city, municipal and provincial level, plus sectoral statutes. Among the localities with a non-discrimination ordinance is Butuan City, the capital of Caraga, adopted in 2016; a visitor's protection therefore varies sharply by which city or municipality they are in. Republic Act 11166 separately prohibits discrimination tied to HIV status, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and the Safe Spaces Act and Magna Carta of Women punish transphobic and homophobic slurs with fines and, in some cases, a sensitivity seminar.

Violence against trans people is documented and recent at national level. In June 2025 two killings occurred within days: 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol was found dead in a Cagayan river on 23 June, and a trans woman former journalist and activist was shot inside a clinic in General Santos the same day. In May 2025 a foreign national was arrested for raping a trans woman in Batangas. The Commission on Human Rights has described that year's killings of trans people as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide.

Public presentation can attract official and private restriction. Marawi City banned men from appearing in public in female attire, makeup or earrings in December 2004, and Kabacan in Cotabato prohibited cross-dressing for Muslims in November 2019 under penalty of imprisonment. Gender-diverse people have been refused entry and service by establishments with little or no legal consequence. A 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets, an attitude that shapes how such refusals are received locally.

Executive measures exist on paper without effect. Executive Order 100 s.2019, signed 17 December 2019, created a Diversity and Inclusion Program, amended by EO 51 s.2023 to add a special LGBTQIA+ affairs committee; neither was implemented as of 2025.

Marriage equality does not exist. The Family Code defines marriage as between a man and a woman, and same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised nationally.
tangentialFactors:
Caraga's profile is a regional illustration of a national pattern rather than an exception: the Philippines decriminalised same-sex conduct and has never criminalised trans identity, yet leaves recognition and protection to a patchwork of local measures. A 2026 travel-risk assessment scores Manila at 69 of 100, 'Generally Safe', for LGBTQ+ travellers overall, but 62 for trans travellers, which falls in the 'Exercise Caution' band; the same assessment scores HIV-positive travellers at 81. The gap between the general and trans-specific scores indicates that a trans visitor faces a measurably higher risk profile than an LGB traveller in the same setting.

Detention carries acute risk nationwide. Transgender women and gay men are held in ordinary male dormitories, including Manila City Jail, where head-sharing on arrival is mandatory for the male dorm and safety depends on inmate hierarchies rather than policy. There is no gender-matched placement; the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology in Davao instead transfers LGBT detainees in batches to a city jail annex alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, to prevent abuse. A trans visitor detained in Caraga should expect placement by birth-assigned sex.

Social visibility is high and cuts both ways. Long-standing gender-diversity traditions with local names such as bakla and tomboy sit alongside prominent Pride events, nightlife and substantial LGBTQ+ media presence. Openly gay and bisexual people have been permitted in the armed forces since 2009 and transgender people since 2017, with uniform policy following the legal gender recorded on the birth certificate. The lawyers' Code of Professional Responsibility was updated in 2023 to bar discrimination against clients on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity. In June 2023 Quezon City launched the country's first Right to Care Card, letting registered LGBTQ couples make medical and health decisions for each other, initially in government-owned hospitals.
localsOnly:
Residents of Caraga live under the same national framework as visitors, but the local ordinance layer matters more to them. Butuan City, Caraga's capital, adopted a non-discrimination ordinance in 2016, one of a set covering eight provinces and 32 cities and municipalities nationwide. National protection remains absent: the SOGIE Equality Bill has been pending in Congress for roughly 25 years, and the protections that do exist form a patchwork of local ordinances and sectoral statutes, including the Magna Carta for Public Social Workers, which penalises SOGIE harassment with a fine of 20,000 to 40,000 pesos and/or up to one year's imprisonment.

Legal gender recognition requires a court order, since the Clerical Error Law forecloses the administrative route and Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) bars change even after gender-affirming surgery. A resident's birth-certificate marker therefore governs uniform policy in the armed forces and, in practice, placement in detention. The Bureau of Jail Management and Penology's batch-transfer practice in Davao is the nearest thing to an official accommodation, and it is segregation rather than gender-matched placement.

Local opinion is not uniformly supportive. A 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found 22% support for same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets. Executive Order 100 s.2019 and its 2023 amendment created a Diversity and Inclusion Program and a special LGBTQIA+ affairs committee, but neither was implemented as of 2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
Two items in the source inventory remain unresolved. The first is whether any Caraga city or province outside Butuan City has adopted a SOGIE or non-discrimination ordinance; the inventory names only Butuan for this region, and the wider national count of eight provinces and 32 cities and municipalities is not broken down by region. The second is whether the trans-specific travel-risk scores (69 and 62 for Manila) have any regional equivalent for Caraga; none is sourced, so the Manila figures are used as a national proxy and may not reflect conditions in Butuan or elsewhere in the region.

The status of the gender-marker bill is stated as of the reports, with allies planning to endorse it to the 20 Congress on 28 July; whether it has advanced since is not sourced here. The Wikipedia entry for Caraga itself records no usable finding on LGBT rights, so the region-specific layer of this dossier rests on the absence of a recorded regulation rather than on an affirmative statement that none exists.
